places.name: Coalinga Oil Field
places.text: The long, low ridge between the freeway and Coalinga is Anticline Ridge, part of the Coalinga Oil Field, one of only six California fields to have produced more than a billion barrels of oil. By 1910 it was the most productive oil field in the state. Long before drillers came, Native people here used tar from natural seeps to line baskets and to trade.
places.more: In September 1909 a well called Silver Tip blew in at 20,000 barrels a day, then the biggest gusher California had seen, and the Los Angeles Stock Exchange closed for a day so its members could take the train to see it. According to a 1905 New York Times article, Standard Oil tried to squeeze out the local independent drillers by holding the price of oil as low as ten cents a barrel. The independents answered by building their own pipeline to San Francisco Bay, working on a dummy pipeline in plain sight while the real one went in quietly. Production peaked in 1912. Highways 33 and 198 cross the field, and travelers on them get a good view of the oil field at work.

places.name: Harris Ranch Inn and restaurant
places.text: The Harris Ranch restaurant opened beside the freeway in 1977, aimed at local farmers, and soon became a popular halfway stop on the drive between Los Angeles and San Francisco. A 153-room hacienda-style inn was added in 1987, and by 2008 the restaurant ranked sixth in California by sales.
places.more: In the late 2000s the restaurant turned to a farm to fork menu, serving the ranch's own beef along with wine and other products the ranch makes. Its beef and prepared meals also go to grocery stores and restaurants across the country. Next to the inn is Harris Ranch Airport, a single runway 2,820 feet long, open since 1981. No planes are based there, yet it averages about 27 takeoffs and landings a day, and one of its most common uses is flying in to eat or stay at Harris Ranch.
places.spot: Look for the big hacienda-style inn right beside the freeway.

places.name: Coalinga and the Iron Zoo
places.text: Coalinga began in 1888 as a Southern Pacific coaling stop for steam locomotives, called Coaling Station A. Local tradition says a railroad official made the name more musical by adding an a. It is just as likely that a small station sign squeezed Coaling A into Coalinga.
places.more: In the early 1970s, Jean Dakessian Jones, whose motel sat empty much of the time after Interstate 5 opened, began painting the nodding oil pumps around town as animals and characters. Her imagination, she said, saw them as all kinds of creatures. Shell's local manager took her idea to the head office, which paid for the paint, and by mid-1973 she had painted all 23 of Shell's pumps. She then held a contest for local artists to paint 34 more. The Iron Zoo grew to include a zebra, a giraffe, a bald eagle and a bobbing goat, and Jones recalled people saying, meet me at the zebra after the game tonight. Many of the painted pumps have since been shut down and taken apart.

places.name: Harris Ranch feedlot
places.text: Harris Ranch is California's largest beef producer, and its feedlot sits right beside the freeway. It holds more than 100,000 cattle on more than 800 acres, so many travelers notice it by smell first. That smell inspired food writer Michael Pollan's research on factory farming, which led to his book The Omnivore's Dilemma.
places.more: Jack Harris and his wife, Teresa, started the ranch in 1937 on 320 acres of desert land that had never been farmed. His parents had come to California's Imperial Valley in 1916 to build one of the state's first cotton gins. At its peak the family company grew more than 33 crops a year, and today its fields grow onions, garlic, almonds, pistachios, lettuce, tomatoes, citrus and melons. A thoroughbred division, started in 1966, raises racehorses. The beef business handles cattle from start to finish, with its own trucks, finishing pens, slaughter and packing.

places.name: The 1983 Coalinga earthquake
places.text: At 4:42 on the afternoon of May 2, 1983, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck Coalinga. The town's eight-block downtown was almost destroyed, with the worst damage to buildings with unreinforced brick walls, and 94 people were injured. The shaking was felt from the Los Angeles area to Susanville, in Lassen County.
places.more: The main shock broke no fault at the surface. Instead, an anticline ridge northeast of town rose about half a meter, roughly a foot and a half. More than 5,000 aftershocks were recorded by the end of July. Newer buildings, like the Bank of America branch, came through with only surface damage, while more than 300 houses were almost destroyed. In the oil fields, pumping units, tanks and pipelines were damaged, and 14 of 1,725 active wells had collapsed or broken casings underground. The quake worried geologists because it raised fears about faults no one had known about.

places.name: Westlands Water District
places.text: Much of the west side of Fresno and Kings counties, along this part of the freeway, is served by Westlands Water District, formed in 1952. By irrigable acres it is the largest farm water district in the country, about 614,000 acres, where roughly 700 farmers own land.
places.more: Farms here first irrigated from deep wells, starting around 1915, and the heavy pumping lowered the water table and made the land sink. Federal water finally arrived through the San Luis Canal, finished in 1968. The government also agreed to build a drain for the salty water that collects under the fields, but only the first part was built. Its water ended up in the ponds of Kesterson Reservoir, and the drainage was shut off in the mid-1980s after selenium in it harmed water birds there. Westlands still has no outlet for that drainage water, and because of its size it sits at the center of many of California's water fights.

places.name: Plane wreck at Los Gatos
places.text: On January 28, 1948, a chartered DC-3 crashed in the Diablo Range about 20 miles west of Coalinga, near Los Gatos Creek. All 32 people aboard died. Most were Mexican farmworkers being sent back to Mexico, some at the end of their bracero contracts. First news reports named only the pilot, copilot, flight attendant and immigration guard, and listed the rest simply as deportees.
places.more: Woody Guthrie wrote a poem about the nameless victims, and a decade later a college student, Martin Hoffman, set it to music. The song, Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos), has been sung by Pete Seeger, Joan Baez, Johnny Cash, Dolly Parton and Bruce Springsteen, among many others. The Mexican victims were buried in a mass grave in Fresno marked only Mexican Nationals. Writer Tim Z. Hernandez began searching for their names in 2009, and on Labor Day 2013 a headstone listing all 28 was unveiled before more than 600 people. News of the crash helped convince a young Cesar Chavez that farmworkers should be treated as important human beings, not as farm tools.

places.name: Joaquin Rocks
places.text: On the high ridge west of the freeway stand three stone pillars, about 4,100 feet up. These are the Joaquin Rocks, once called Las Tres Piedras, the Three Rocks, and they can be seen for miles across the valley. They are named for the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta, whose gang is said to have used them as a lookout.
places.more: From their tops the rocks look out over much of the San Joaquin Valley, including the approaches to Arroyo de Cantua, where the gang kept its rancho. In 1954 a man named Raymond Minnite, from Hiawatha, Utah, sat at a crossroads east of the freeway, counting passing cars and dreaming about how many he could get to stop. He noticed the three rocks on the skyline and named the little town he founded there Three Rocks. About 250 people lived there in 2020.
places.spot: Look for three rock pillars standing on top of the high ridge to the west.

places.name: Arroyo de Cantua
places.text: Where Cantua Creek leaves the hills, about a mile and a half west of the freeway, is Arroyo de Cantua, said to be the hideout of the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta. On July 25, 1853, California Rangers led by Captain Harry Love attacked a band of armed Mexican men near here, killed three, and claimed one of them was Murrieta.
places.more: As proof, the rangers cut off the head they said was Murrieta's and the hand of his associate Three-Fingered Jack, and kept them in a jar of alcohol to collect their reward. The jar toured California, and people paid a dollar to look. That August, a letter to a San Francisco newspaper claimed the rangers had killed innocent mustang catchers. Evidence for a real Murrieta is thin, but the legend grew, helped along by an 1854 novel by John Rollin Ridge, a Cherokee writer. The head was destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire.

places.name: Mendota, cantaloupe town
places.text: Highway 33 leads from here to Mendota, known as the Cantaloupe Center of the World. It began to thrive in 1891 as a Southern Pacific storage and switching yard, and the railroad borrowed its name from Mendota, Illinois. The town sits beside the San Joaquin River, near where the Delta-Mendota Canal pours in water to refill a riverbed that is often dry.
places.more: Mendota Dam, built in 1871 where the river meets Fresno Slough, first sent water into the Main Canal for riverside farmland. Since 1951 the Delta-Mendota Canal has ended at the pool behind it, bringing Delta water through 117 miles of canal from near Tracy. Fresno Slough can flow either way: north into the river in the rainy season, and south toward the Tulare Lake basin in the dry months. In the years after the Gold Rush, a nearby settlement called Las Juntas was a haven for fugitives, visited by the bandits Joaquin Murrieta and Tiburcio Vasquez.

places.name: The nation's top farm county
places.text: Fresno County, which the freeway crosses here, was the number one farm county in the nation in 2017, when its crops and livestock were worth almost 8 billion dollars. About 1.9 million acres, nearly half the county, are farmed. More than 300 crops grow here, and the leaders range from grapes, pistachios and almonds to tomatoes, cotton and milk.
places.more: Pistachios have spread widely. California's pistachio orchards grew from about 106,000 acres in 2002 to 554,000 acres in 2022, because the hardy trees can thrive with the somewhat salty water and soil found in parts of the Central Valley. Fresno County alone grew about 40 percent of the country's pistachios in 2021, and in 2017 it ranked second in the state for cotton. In 2000 the county used more fresh water each day than any other county in the United States, about 3.7 billion gallons.

places.name: The 1991 dust storm
places.text: On November 29, 1991, the Friday after Thanksgiving, a sudden dust storm swept this stretch of I-5 north of Coalinga and dropped visibility to near zero. In a series of chain-reaction crashes, 104 vehicles collided, 17 people died and 150 were hurt. The Highway Patrol called it the deadliest dust storm crash in state history.
places.more: The valley was in its sixth year of drought, the rainy season had not begun, and fields near the road had been plowed and left bare, with no crops to hold the dust. The nearest weather station tracking wind, at Naval Air Station Lemoore, recorded gusts of 48 miles an hour. Most of the crashes happened in five groups along a mile and a half of freeway, and several vehicles caught fire. A fire truck and an ambulance crashed on the way in, yet rescuers reached the site within half an hour. About 150 miles of I-5 were closed for a day.

places.name: The Diablo Range
places.text: The mountains west of the freeway are the Diablo Range, part of California's Coast Ranges. It stretches from the Carquinez Strait, near the Bay Area, south to Polonio Pass, near Cholame. Its highest point, San Benito Mountain, rises to 5,241 feet in remote country to the southwest.
places.more: Other coastal ranges to the west catch most of the ocean's rain, so these mountains stay dry, mostly rolling grassland, chaparral and oak woodland, and most of the land is private ranches. The range is part of the homelands of many Native peoples, including the Ohlone, Yokuts, Miwok, Amah Mutsun and Salinan. It also shelters a millipede found only in the southern part of the range, Illacme plenipes, which can have as many as 750 legs. Until 2021, no animal known to science had more. It was first found in 1926 and not seen again until 2005.

places.name: El Camino Viejo
places.text: Long before the freeway, an older road ran along this side of the valley: El Camino Viejo, the Old Road to Los Angeles. Spanish ox carts used it as early as 1780, traveling from one creek or waterhole to the next along the foot of the Coast Ranges, between San Pedro Bay and the shore of San Francisco Bay at Oakland.
places.more: Its Spanish names for creeks and watering places described what travelers found: Arroyo de las Garzas, Creek of the Herons, and Aguaje de las Berendas, Waterhole of the Pronghorns, in Merced County, and Arroyo de las Polvarduras, Creek of the Dust Storms, in Fresno County. The road was favored by those who wanted to stay out of sight of Spanish officials on the coast. Later, Californio vaqueros drove cattle along it, while mustang catchers herded wild horses to the Bay Area, Southern California and Sonora. At its north end the road turned west over the Diablo Range at Corral Hollow Pass. Through Santa Nella, its route has been replaced by Interstate 5 and Highway 33.

places.name: The sinking ground
places.text: Southwest of Mendota, east of the freeway, the ground sank about 28 feet between 1925 and 1977 because so much groundwater was pumped from under the fields. A famous photo shows U.S. Geological Survey scientist Joseph Poland beside a utility pole there, with signs high on the pole marking where the ground surface was in 1925 and 1955.
places.more: Poland spent 50 years studying sinking land and became known as Mr. Land Subsidence. When too much groundwater is pumped out, loose layers underground compact, and past a certain point the ground cannot spring back. The sinking began in the 1920s, and by 1970 more than a foot of it had spread across about 5,200 square miles, about half the valley. It was first discovered in the 1950s, and a network to measure it was built in the 1960s. The sinking has cut how much water the Delta-Mendota Canal can carry and has meant expensive repairs to canals, including the California Aqueduct.

places.name: Panoche Hills
places.text: The low hills west of the freeway are the Panoche Hills, rising east of the higher Diablo Range. Their name is thought to come from a local Native word for a cane that once grew in the valley beyond them, from which people made panoche, a kind of sugar.
places.more: West of the hills lies Panoche Valley, home to endangered animals such as the San Joaquin kit fox, the giant kangaroo rat and the blunt-nosed leopard lizard. Its grasslands are critical habitat, especially in winter, for birds such as golden eagles, ferruginous hawks, prairie falcons, mountain plovers and long-billed curlews. The hills themselves hold fossils of ancient cold seeps from the Mesozoic era, the age of dinosaurs. The Bureau of Land Management keeps motor vehicles out of its Panoche Hills recreation area from mid-April to mid-October, the fire season.

places.name: Panoche Creek and the mercury mines
places.text: Panoche Creek, which comes out of the hills near here, drains a larger area than any other stream on the Diablo Range's eastern slope. Its old Spanish name was Arroyo de Panoche Grande, Big Sugarloaf Creek. It was part of a route between Native settlements on the central coast and the valley, and a watering place on El Camino Viejo.
places.more: Far upstream, in the southern Diablo Range near its highest peak, are the old New Idria mines, which dug mercury from 1854 until 1972 and were at one time the second most productive mercury mines in the country. Gold Rush miners needed mercury to pull gold out of ore, and before New Idria and New Almaden it came almost entirely from Europe. The mines left behind a ghost town with more than 100 standing buildings, and mercury from the old workings has polluted the creeks that feed Panoche Creek. In 2011 the site was listed for federal Superfund cleanup.

places.name: Mercey Hot Springs
places.text: On Little Panoche Road, in the hills west of the freeway, Mercey Hot Springs has been a resort since the early 1900s. Water flows from one spring at 119 degrees Fahrenheit, and the resort has cabins, campsites, bathtub soaking pools and a swimming pool fed by a hot artesian well.
places.more: Native people knew the springs long before settlers came, and they showed them to a sheepherder named John Merci, who later spelled his name Mercy. During the Gold Rush the spot was a watering place called Aguaje Panochita, where mustang catchers held captured horses, and it was a stop for the gang known as the Five Joaquins as they drove horses south to their hideout on Cantua Creek. In 1912 San Francisco developer Frederick Bourn bought the springs and built cabins and a hotel. The hotel burned in the mid-1930s and was replaced by a bathhouse and restaurant. Little Panoche Road itself was once part of a stagecoach route.

places.name: The San Luis Canal
places.text: The big canal on this part of the drive is officially the San Luis Canal, the federally built section of the California Aqueduct. It carries water for both the state and federal water projects from O'Neill Forebay to Kettleman City, and with room for 13,100 cubic feet of water a second, it is one of the largest irrigation canals in the country.
places.more: Little Panoche Creek, which comes out of the hills near here, shows how much the canals have changed the land. Before irrigation, its water may have reached a slough of the San Joaquin River in very wet years. Today it flows through Little Panoche Reservoir and simply ends in the aqueduct. Its old Spanish name, Arroyita de Panoche, meant Little Sugarloaf Creek, and it was a watering place on El Camino Viejo.

places.name: Firebaugh's Ferry
places.text: East of the freeway, on the San Joaquin River, is Firebaugh, named for Andrew Firebaugh, a Virginian who ran a ferry across the river during the Gold Rush. The settlement, then called Firebaugh's Ferry, became a station on the Butterfield Overland stage line. A water tank in its small downtown is painted with the city's name.
places.more: In 1857 Firebaugh built a wagon road with a gentler grade over Pacheco Pass, replacing a steep, rough horse and mule trail that ran near today's Highway 152. In the 1880s the land around his ferry was part of the huge holdings of Miller and Lux, whose cattle operation covered the country from Dos Palos to Mendota. Firebaugh became a city in 1914. It holds a yearly Cantaloupe Round-Up to celebrate the melon harvest, which peaks in late July.

places.name: John Chuck Erreca Rest Area
places.text: Caltrans rebuilt both sides of the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area in a 30 million dollar project, reopening one side in August 2025 and the other in May 2026. Caltrans calls it one of the most sustainable rest areas it has ever built, with utilities designed to use little water and power.
places.more: A small treatment system cleans gray water so it can be used again to flush the toilets, which cuts the rest area's need for water from the state system during droughts. The landscaping uses native, drought-tolerant plants, the plaza's design was inspired by aerial views of farmland, and graphics honor the region's Basque history. The parking areas took more than 180,000 cubic feet of concrete, 9 inches thick for cars and 12 inches thick for trucks. That light-colored concrete reflects sunlight, which helps keep the air cooler.

places.name: The San Joaquin River
places.text: East of the freeway, the San Joaquin River winds past Firebaugh. The southern Yokuts name for it, Tihshachu, means salmon-spearing place. Its Spanish name dates to explorer Gabriel Moraga, who named one of its branches for Saint Joachim between 1805 and 1808, and the name was in common use by 1810.
places.more: Before irrigation, the San Joaquin and its branches had the third largest salmon run in California, likely 200,000 to 500,000 spawning fish a year. With most of its water now held behind Friant Dam and sent into canals, long stretches often run dry. In 2009 the federal government began releasing water from Friant again to restore two dry stretches, about 64 miles in all, part of one of the largest river recovery efforts in the country, with salmon to be brought back. Not everyone welcomed it: irrigators lost some water, and a lawsuit claimed the new flows were seeping through old levees onto farmland near Los Banos.

places.name: Dos Amigos Pumping Plant
places.text: Beside the freeway, the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant lifts California Aqueduct water 118 feet. Its six pumps can move 15,450 cubic feet of water a second, and that single boost lets the water flow by gravity for about 95 miles, to where the aqueduct's Coastal Branch splits off south of Kettleman City.
places.more: The plant was built between 1963 and 1966 as part of the State Water Project, and its name means two friends in Spanish. Its water arrives through about 16 miles of canal from O'Neill Forebay. After the Coastal Branch split, the main aqueduct runs by gravity for another 66 miles to the Buena Vista Pumping Plant, which gives it the next lift. A vista point called Dos Amigos sits beside the freeway nearby.
places.spot: Look for a big pumping plant beside the wide concrete canal.

places.name: The Grasslands
places.text: East of the freeway lie the Grasslands, about 250 square miles of wetlands and grasslands along the San Joaquin River, named a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar treaty. They sit on the Pacific Flyway, the great bird migration route, and are important habitat for resident and migrating water birds.
places.more: Each autumn more than 20,000 cranes and 60,000 Arctic-nesting geese fly in from Alaska and Canada to spend about six months at Merced National Wildlife Refuge, part of the Grasslands. It holds the largest wintering flocks of lesser sandhill cranes and Ross's geese on the Pacific Flyway. The refuge was set up in 1951 to draw wintering ducks and geese away from nearby farm fields, where they were damaging crops. In spring, wildflowers bloom in rings around drying vernal pools, the kind of color that led John Muir to call the valley floor the floweriest part of the world he had seen.

places.name: Path 15 power lines
places.text: Path 15, part of California's main north-south power corridor, runs along this side of the valley, generally 3 to 7 miles west of the freeway. Its 500,000-volt lines run from the Los Banos substation, west of Los Banos, to Midway, near Buttonwillow, linking hydroelectric plants in the north with fossil fuel power plants in the south.
places.more: In places the lines run beside the freeway, and the two eastern lines cross it twice. Between Los Banos and the Gates substation near Coalinga there were once only two 500,000-volt lines, a bottleneck that was one of the leading causes of California's electricity crisis of 2000 and 2001. A third line, built by the federal Western Area Power Administration with several utilities, was finished on time and under budget on December 21, 2004. It runs apart from the other two, often out of sight, and it is the only line in Path 15 that strings its wires in bundles of three. North of Los Banos, two of the corridor's lines cross O'Neill Forebay on several man-made islands.

places.name: Los Banos, the baths
places.text: Los Banos, the city about 7 miles east of the freeway, is Spanish for the baths. It is named for pools known as the baths of Padre Arroyo, a regular stop for priests from Mission San Juan Bautista on trips into the valley, visited by Spanish explorers as early as 1805. Later settlers called the stream Los Banos Creek, and the post office and town took the name too.
places.more: The town moved to its present site in 1889, when the railroad arrived. Cattle baron Henry Miller ran his valley empire from Canal Farm here, set up in 1873, and in the late 1800s he was one of the largest landowners in the United States. Uriah Wood, the area's first Anglo-American settler, once raced Miller to the land office in Stockton to file a claim. After crossing the San Joaquin River, Wood paid the ferryman five dollars to hold the boat on the east side, and won his land for 45 cents an acre. A 10-acre plaza downtown honors Miller with a big bronze of him and his cattle.

places.name: Tomato country
places.text: The Morning Star Company, which opened its first tomato factory in Los Banos in 1990 and another at Santa Nella in 2002, was the world's leading tomato processor as of 2023. It handles about 5 million tons of tomatoes a year, roughly 40 percent of California's processing tomato crop, for products like tomato paste and diced tomatoes.
places.more: Chris Rufer started Morning Star in 1970 as an owner-operator trucker, hauling tomatoes from fields to canneries. The company is known for having no bosses: workers define their own job duties, and pay is based on reviews from coworkers. Its factories can handle more than 3,000 tons of tomatoes an hour, and at harvest time more than 2,500 seasonal workers join about 550 year-round employees. As of 2023 it supplied about a tenth of the world's ingredient tomato products.

places.name: Pacheco Pass
places.text: Highway 152 heads west over Pacheco Pass, at 1,368 feet the main route through the hills between the Central Valley and the Santa Clara Valley. Yokuts people used a trail nearby to cross the mountains and trade with Native people on the coast, and Spanish officer Gabriel Moraga first recorded the pass in 1805.
places.more: The pass is named for Francisco Perez Pacheco, a Californio rancher. In the 1850s travelers called it Robber's Pass because of frequent holdups. Pacheco Pass Station was a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoach route, which linked St. Louis with San Francisco from 1858 to 1861. California's high-speed rail line is planned to run beneath the pass in the Pacheco Pass Tunnels, about 13 miles long, which are expected to be the longest rail tunnels in North America.

places.name: Tule elk at San Luis refuge
places.text: About 13 miles east, San Luis National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1967, keeps a herd of reintroduced tule elk, the smallest kind of elk, found only in California. About half a million tule elk roamed the state when Europeans arrived, but by 1870 they were thought to be gone.
places.more: In 1874 the cattle king Henry Miller found a few survivors on his ranch near Bakersfield and protected them, and by 1895 there were 28. Reintroductions later spread herds around the state. In March 1978, ten tule elk from Merced County, two males and eight females, were moved to Tomales Point at Point Reyes, where the herd struggled at first, then began growing fast in 1981. By 2019 California had about 5,700 tule elk. At the refuge, visitors can drive a Tule Elk auto tour route, and in hot months the elk are easiest to see in the morning or early evening.

places.name: San Luis Reservoir
places.text: West of the freeway, B.F. Sisk Dam, 382 feet high and more than three and a half miles long, holds back San Luis Reservoir, the largest offstream reservoir in the nation. Most of its water does not flow in from a river at all: it is pumped in from canals fed by the Delta and stored for the dry months.
places.more: On August 18, 1962, President John F. Kennedy and Governor Pat Brown gave the signal for the first blasts at the dam site, in front of 15,000 people. The valley it flooded is Yokuts homeland, later part of Rancho San Luis Gonzaga, and the reservoir first filled on May 31, 1969. Between the dam and O'Neill Forebay, the Gianelli Pumping-Generating Plant works like a giant water battery. When demand for electricity is low, its eight reversible units pump water up into the reservoir, and when demand is high, the water runs back down through the same machines, which can make 424 megawatts. Only about 70 percent of the pumping energy comes back, but selling power at peak times helps pay for the State Water Project's giant pumps. A plan approved in 2023 would raise the dam 10 feet by 2032.

places.name: Pea Soup Andersen's
places.text: Pea Soup Andersen's opened here in 1976 as the second location of a roadside restaurant famous for its pea soup. When the 1924 original in Buellton closed in January 2024, just before its 100th anniversary, this became the only Pea Soup Andersen's left. Its working windmill can be seen from the freeway.
places.more: Danish-born Anton Andersen and his French-born wife, Juliette, opened their first cafe in 1924 and named it for their proudest possession, a new electric stove. Pea soup, made from a recipe handed down in Juliette's family, went on the menu three months later. Their son Robert later called himself Pea Soup Andersen, and the mascots Hap-pea and Pea-wee, two cartoon chefs splitting peas with a hammer and chisel, came from a cartoon by Charles Forbell. Opening day in Santa Nella drew more than 10,000 customers, and the 77-foot windmill still turns whenever the restaurant is open.
places.spot: Look for a tall windmill on the restaurant near the Santa Nella exit.

places.name: Santa Nella's name
places.text: Santa Nella sounds like a saint's name, but there is no Saint Nella. The name is an English mangling of the Spanish word centinela, sentinel, from Rancho de Centinela, a horse ranch started here in 1810 by stockmen from San Juan Bautista and Monterey.
places.more: The ranch failed after many of its horses escaped into the valley, followed by fighting with Native people. The spot stayed a stopping place: it sat on El Camino Viejo, and in the Gold Rush the stage road from Hill's Ferry crossed San Luis Creek here on its way to Pacheco Pass. Basque sheepmen built a two-story adobe nearby in the 1860s, and Miller and Lux later replaced it with a frame house that stood until the 1960s, when a roadside stop took its place. Santa Nella is still mostly a place for travelers to stop.

places.name: San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery
places.text: West of the freeway, on McCabe Road near Santa Nella, is San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery, on land the Romero Ranch Company donated in 1989. It covers 322 acres, its first section was finished in 1992, and more than 30,000 burials had taken place there by 2008.
places.more: Its California Korean War Veterans Memorial, set up in 1998, is a circle of 16 granite pillars, each five feet tall, engraved with the names of the 2,495 Californians who died in the Korean War. An 11th Airborne memorial, dedicated in 2002, honors all airborne forces, and a small museum on the grounds displays uniforms and medals. Among those buried here is Seaman William Troy, who received the Medal of Honor for action against Korean forts in 1871, 79 years before the Korean War began. Boxer Mac Foster, a Marine sergeant, is buried here too.

places.name: Two canals side by side
places.text: Two big canals run side by side along the western edge of the valley between here and Tracy: the state's California Aqueduct and the federal Delta-Mendota Canal. The Delta-Mendota, finished in 1951, starts at a pumping plant near Tracy that lifts water 197 feet out of the Delta, and it runs 117 miles to the San Joaquin River near Mendota.
places.more: The canal exists because of a water swap. Friant Dam, far up the San Joaquin, sends that river's water into canals serving the east side of the valley, so the Delta-Mendota brings Sacramento River water from the Delta to replace it for farms downstream. Its builders worked three shifts a day, 21 hours a day, six days a week. Later the ground beneath it sank, more than 6 feet along its southern 30 to 40 miles, and the changes in elevation were at first blamed on earthquakes. In places the sinking left bridges, pipes and even cattle guards underwater.

places.name: The first West Side Freeway
places.text: This part of I-5, between Los Banos and the San Joaquin County line, was the first stretch of the West Side Freeway to be finished, in 1967. Planners chose this remote side of the valley over turning Highway 99 into a freeway, because it skipped the farm towns and gave a faster, more direct route through the state.
places.more: Local groups had pushed for a west side freeway as early as 1945, and construction began in the early 1960s. The rest came in two big pieces: the stretch to Wheeler Ridge in 1972 and the one to Sacramento in 1979. When the long southern section opened in 1972, there were no businesses beside it and the nearest towns were miles away and out of sight, so cars often ran out of gas. The median from Wheeler Ridge to Tracy is wide enough that the freeway could someday grow to six or eight lanes. The stretch from Highway 152 near Santa Nella to I-580 near Tracy is an official state scenic highway.

places.name: Kesterson and the selenium birds
places.text: About 11 miles east is Kesterson Reservoir, now part of San Luis National Wildlife Refuge. In 1983 scientists found that 64 percent of the water bird embryos and hatchlings there were deformed or dead, poisoned by selenium in farm drainage water. The discovery drew national attention, and the ponds were closed in 1986.
places.more: Kesterson's 12 ponds were the temporary end of the San Luis Drain, planned to run 290 miles and carry away salty water from under west side fields. Only 82 miles were built before work stopped in 1975, so the drainage collected at Kesterson and evaporated, concentrating selenium that had washed out of black shale in the Coast Ranges. Birds hatched with missing or deformed eyes, beaks, wings and legs. Cleanup crews filled 713 acres with about a million cubic yards of soil, and scientists now call selenium's path from rock to duck the Kesterson effect.

places.name: Gustine
places.text: The town of Gustine, east of the freeway, is named for Sara Miller, the daughter of cattle king Henry Miller. Her middle name was Augustine and her nickname was Gussie, and she died at eight after being thrown from her horse. Gustine grew up in the early 1900s as a Southern Pacific station, opened its post office in 1907 and became a city in 1915.
places.more: In March 1970 Gustine became the first place in California with a 9-1-1 emergency phone system. The town is home to a festa steeped in Portuguese tradition that is described as the largest in the nation. Gustine High School hosts what is called the longest-running basketball tournament in California. The local Rotary Club puts it on, and it celebrated its 75th year in 2017.

places.name: Hills Ferry
places.text: About 7 miles east, where the Merced River meets the San Joaquin, stood Hills Ferry, a river crossing started in 1850 and taken over by Jesse Hill in 1854. By the late 1870s it was a busy grain shipping town of several hundred people. When the railroad came through Newman in 1888, Hills Ferry quickly faded away.
places.more: In May 1868 the naturalist John Muir crossed the river here on his long walk from Oakland to Yosemite. Simon Newman's company store stood in Hills Ferry, and the building later served as Fisher's Opera House until it was torn down in 1904. In July 1906 a fire near Hills Ferry and Newman burned 2,500 acres of wheat and barley and 20,000 acres of pasture. By 1976, not even the shadows of a ghost town were left.

places.name: Newman and Orestimba Creek
places.text: The town of Newman, east of the freeway, was founded in 1888 by Simon Newman, a businessman who came to California from Bavaria as a teenager in 1862. Born Simon Neumann, he arrived speaking only German and Hebrew, learned English, and translated his family name.
places.more: Orestimba Creek, which comes down from the Diablo Range near here, has the largest watershed of the 13 streams that feed the San Joaquin from its west side. Its name was first written down as Arroyo de Orestimac in 1810, in the diary of Padre Jose Viader, the longtime head of Mission Santa Clara. The creek watered the Mexican-era Rancho Orestimba y Las Garzas, whose ranch house stood above a sycamore grove on its banks. In 1998 The Nature Conservancy bought the 33,000-acre Simon Newman Ranch in the hills upstream, and it still manages the land.

places.name: Almond bloom
places.text: Almonds are the top farm product of Stanislaus County, which the freeway crosses here. Each February, the pollination of California's almonds is the largest managed pollination event in the world: more than a million beehives, nearly half of all the hives in the country, are trucked in to the orchards.
places.more: Most almond varieties cannot pollinate themselves, so growers plant a mix of varieties and count on bees to carry pollen between them. Pollination brokers hire migratory beekeepers from at least 49 states for the job. In 2017 California had about a million acres of almonds, which produced 2.25 billion pounds of shelled nuts. When colony collapse disorder caused a shortage of honey bees around the turn of this century, government scientists developed almond trees that can pollinate themselves.

places.name: Crows Landing airfield
places.text: East of the freeway is the old Crows Landing airfield. The Navy broke ground on December 1, 1942, and trained pilots here in Wildcat and Avenger warplanes during World War Two, later adding big patrol bombers. NASA's Ames Research Center took it over in 1993, and in 2022 the county announced plans to turn it into a business park.
places.more: Crows Landing itself began as a landing on the San Joaquin River, started by John Crow, who came west from Missouri by covered wagon. His father had left Missouri for the gold fields in 1849. In 1887 the town moved four miles west to be on the Southern Pacific railroad, and members of the Crow family still farm walnuts there. During the war the Navy ran ten liberty buses a day to Modesto and Patterson for its sailors, who were allowed to use the swimming pool at Patterson High School.

places.name: Diablo Grande
places.text: Diablo Grande Parkway leads into the Diablo Range to Diablo Grande, a gated hillside community about 9 miles southwest of Patterson, at 1,535 feet. Developer Donald Panoz dreamed of a resort town with up to 10,000 homes, six golf courses, a resort hotel and spa, vineyards and a winery.
places.more: The plan ran into trouble early. By 1999 a court had rejected the project's environmental report, in part because it had not shown where its water would come from, so the developers set up their own water district and arranged transfers of water from farmland. After about 120 million dollars of investment, the owners filed for bankruptcy in March 2008, with about 350 homes built. A golf course designed by Jack Nicklaus and Gene Sarazen closed in 2014 during the drought, and the last course closed in 2019. In August 2020 the community was ordered to evacuate for about a day as the SCU Lightning Complex fires burned in the hills.

places.name: Patterson, the Paris plan
places.text: Thomas Patterson wanted his town to look different from other farm towns, so he laid it out like Washington, D.C., and Paris, with circles and streets spreading out like spokes, and its main streets were planted with palms, eucalyptus and sycamores. In 1971 its chamber of commerce named Patterson the Apricot Capital of the World.
places.more: The land was once the Mexican-era Rancho Del Puerto, granted in 1844. John D. Patterson bought it in 1866 for 5,400 dollars, and by his death in 1902 his holdings had grown to 18,462 acres. Sales of farms and town lots began in 1909, and Patterson became a city in 1919. Its Apricot Fiesta, held on the first weekend of June since 1971, started when California grew 95 percent of the nation's apricots. Today the town is also known for its distribution centers.

places.name: Del Puerto Canyon
places.text: West of Patterson, Del Puerto Canyon cuts into the Diablo Range. Spanish travelers called its creek Arroyo de La Puerta, the Creek of the Door, for the narrow gap where it squeezes out of the canyon into the valley. This is the homeland of the Hoyumne and Miumne, Northern Valley Yokuts peoples, who left grinding rocks and a path carved into the Gateway rocks at the canyon's mouth.
places.more: Many of the canyon's place names, like Hideout Canyon and Murderers Gulch, recall Gold Rush bandits, and Joaquin Murrieta is said to have hidden wild mustangs up Adobe Creek before driving them to Sonora. In June 1862, William Brewer camped in the canyon and wrote in his book Up and Down California of meeting a herd of thirty or forty antelope, as fleet as the wind. A spring up the canyon, Adobe Springs, gives magnesium-rich water that is sold to the 7 Up bottling plant in Modesto. Del Puerto Canyon Road follows the creek west into the mountains.

places.name: The 2020 lightning fires
places.text: In August 2020 a cluster of wildfires burned through the Diablo Range west of the freeway. The SCU Lightning Complex burned nearly 400,000 acres, more than 600 square miles, across six counties between August 16 and October 1, one of the largest wildfires in modern California history.
places.more: The fires reached Lick Observatory on Mount Hamilton on August 20, but the telescope domes did not burn. Two of its three zones, the Canyon and Calaveras zones, grew together into a single fire. In all, 222 buildings were destroyed and six people were hurt, but no one died. A year later, a study of 6,000 acres of East Bay parkland found that the burn had been mostly good for the land: its moderate to low heat spared most trees, renewed the plants and set off the sprouting of rare fire poppies.

places.name: The Westley tire fire
places.text: On September 22, 1999, lightning struck a huge pile of about six million old tires near Westley. The fire burned for 34 days, and the melting rubber turned into at least 250,000 gallons of oil. Cleanup was estimated to cost more than 20 million dollars.
places.more: Waste tires had been stockpiled at the Westley site since the 1960s and were used to fuel a waste-to-energy operation. The fire poured tons of smoke and pollutants into the air and threatened surface water and groundwater. In April 2000 the state sued the landowners, waste tire haulers and waste-to-energy operators to make them pay for the cleanup, saying workers had failed to quickly turn on the site's water cannon and foam systems. Attorney General Bill Lockyer said the tire inferno left behind contaminated soil and threats to groundwater.

places.name: Mount Diablo
places.text: On clear days a lone, double-peaked mountain stands on the northwest skyline: Mount Diablo, 3,849 feet tall and about 40 miles away. In 1851 Colonel Leander Ransom chose its south peak as the starting point for land surveys, and land in most of Northern California and all of Nevada is still described from it.
places.more: The Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone call the mountain Tuyshtak, meaning at the dawn of time, and in Miwok and Ohlone tradition it was the place of creation. Most of the mountain, including its peak, was the homeland of the Volvon, a Bay Miwok-speaking people. The mountain is still growing, pushed up by a hidden thrust fault beneath it. In 1928 Standard Oil put a 10-million-candlepower aviation beacon on top, the Eye of Diablo, which could be seen for a hundred miles. Every year since 1964, Pearl Harbor survivors and their families have relit the beacon on Pearl Harbor Day.
places.spot: On a clear day, look for a lone two-peaked mountain far off to the northwest.

places.name: The I-580 junction
places.text: At this junction, I-580 heads for the Bay Area over Altamont Pass, a major crossing of the Diablo Range. Early plans made it a branch of I-5 called I-5W, and I-5W signs once stood along the road between Tracy and Oakland. The 1964 renumbering dropped the I-5W name, and the route became I-580.
places.more: One stretch of I-580 is named the William Elton Brownie Brown Freeway, for a Tracy man who helped decide the route of I-5 through the San Joaquin Valley. The piece between the I-205 split and this junction was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s on new right-of-way through low hills near Patterson. In all, I-580 runs about 76 miles, from San Rafael through Oakland to this meeting with I-5 south of Tracy. The junction sits in San Joaquin County, just north of the Stanislaus County line.

places.name: San Joaquin River refuge
places.text: East of the freeway, where the Tuolumne and Stanislaus rivers join the San Joaquin, San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge protects more than 7,000 acres of river woodland, wetlands and grassland. It was set up in 1987 to protect the winter home of the Aleutian cackling goose, then endangered, and it has played a major part in the bird's recovery.
places.more: A nonprofit, River Partners, led the planting of about 400,000 native trees across 1,700 acres of the river's floodplain, one of California's largest projects to bring back streamside forest. Swainson's hawks nest in the tall cottonwoods, and herons and cormorants nest together in big oaks on Christman Island. Endangered riparian brush rabbits, raised in captivity, have been returned to their old habitat here. From autumn through spring, big flocks of geese and sandhill cranes gather on the refuge.
places.wiki: San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge

places.name: Vernalis
places.text: Highway 33 leads to Vernalis, east of the freeway, whose name is Latin for springlike. Local historian Earle Williams said it was named after two ranchers' daughters, Verna Carpenter and Alice Hamilton. Its post office began in 1851 at nearby San Joaquin City and moved here in 1888.
places.more: That post office had closed in 1852 and reopened in 1874 before the move. During World War Two, Vernalis had a Navy airfield, Naval Auxiliary Air Station Vernalis, along with a reconditioning center and a camp for prisoners of war. San Joaquin City, near where the Stanislaus River joins the San Joaquin, was probably the largest of the boomtowns that sprang up after the Gold Rush. It was founded in 1851 and kept its size until 1880, when competition from Stockton drew its trade away.

places.name: Estanislao's river
places.text: A few miles east, the Stanislaus River flows into the San Joaquin. The river is named for Estanislao, the baptized name of Cucunuchi, a leader of the Lakisamni, a Yokuts people, and a Native official at Mission San Jose. In the late 1820s he left the mission with about 400 followers and led raids on missions and settlers, until a Mexican army under Mariano Vallejo drove his people from the river in 1829.
places.more: Estanislao trained his fighters in tactics learned from Spanish and Mexican soldiers, digging trenches and building palisades, and at one time he led as many as 4,000 men, including Chumash and other Yokuts. Legend says he carved an S to mark his raids, and he is thought to be one of the inspirations for Zorro. After the final battle, soldiers executed four captured men, and an investigation found one soldier guilty. Mexico never again tried to control the eastern San Joaquin Valley, and the river was renamed in his honor. Estanislao was pardoned in 1829, and he spent his last years at Mission San Jose teaching others the Yokuts language and culture until his death in 1838.

places.name: Tule fog
places.text: From November through March, this part of the valley can fill with tule fog, a thick ground fog named for the tule marshes of the Central Valley. Visibility in it is usually less than 600 feet, and as of 2005 it was the leading cause of weather-related crashes in California.
places.more: It forms after a good rain, on calm winter nights when the damp ground cools quickly and cold air gets trapped under warmer air above. Once settled, it can sit for days or even weeks. The fog matters to farmers too: it helps orchards of almonds, cherries and pistachios get the winter chill they need. Fog days in the valley have dropped by almost half since 1981, partly because cleaner air leaves fewer tiny particles for fog droplets to form on.

places.name: Banta
places.text: West of the freeway is Banta, a settlement dating to the 1840s. In stagecoach days it was the last stop before Altamont Pass on the road between Stockton and the Bay Area. Henry Banta bought its inn in 1863 and changed the sign to read Banta's White House, and travelers soon called the whole place Bantas.
places.more: In 1869 Banta became a stop on the new Western Pacific Railroad, part of the transcontinental line's route from Sacramento over Altamont Pass to the Bay Area. In 1878 the railroad built its new junction at Tracy instead, and Banta became a quiet village at the far edge of the rail yards. The Banta Inn, established in 1879, is said by some locals to be haunted. Steve Perry, later the lead singer of Journey, once called Banta home, and his band Alien Project formed there in the mid-1970s.

places.name: Tracy, the railroad town
places.text: Tracy, west of the freeway, was born on September 8, 1878, when a Southern Pacific line from Oakland was joined to the Central Pacific line there, east of Altamont Pass. The Tracy Historical Museum says the junction was named for Lathrop J. Tracy, a railroad executive from back east.
places.more: Three miles west was the railroad town of Ellis, a coaling station where helper engines were kept to push trains over Altamont Pass; by 1870 it had about 45 buildings. Once the railroad moved its facilities to the new Tracy station, railroad families and businesses followed, and Ellis faded. In 1894 the railroad's local headquarters moved from Lathrop to Tracy, and a roundhouse followed in 1896. By the 1950s farming had become Tracy's main business, and since the 1970s Bay Area growth spilling over the Altamont has made the railroad town a city of more than 90,000. This is Yokuts homeland, and Yokuts people still live in the region.

places.name: San Joaquin County farms
places.text: San Joaquin County, which the freeway crosses here, is a major national center of farming. In its 2024 crop report, milk was the top commodity and almonds came second, with walnuts fifth and cherries sixth. The county also has more acres of wine grapes than any other county in California.
places.more: Farming became the county's main business in the 1870s, as the Gold Rush economy faded, helped by the reclaiming of Delta marshland that began in 1869. In 2024 its farms produced about 3.1 billion dollars' worth of crops and livestock. The county grows about half of California's cherries, and its more than a dozen cherry packing houses handle nearly all the cherries grown in the state. It is also home to one of the largest walnut processing plants in the world, a major handler of Livermore red walnuts, a variety developed in the San Joaquin Valley.

zones.label: Coalinga plains
zones.text: Wide-open farmland stretches east of the freeway, with the oil field ridges around Coalinga and the Diablo Range to the west, and the big Harris Ranch feedlot beside the freeway often announces itself by smell.

seasons.summer: Summers around Coalinga are very hot and dry, and most of its 8 inches of yearly rain falls from October to May.

zones.label: Westlands farm country
zones.text: Big farms of Westlands Water District spread across the valley floor here, growing crops such as almonds, tomatoes, pistachios and wheat, with the three Joaquin Rocks on the ridge to the west.

seasons.winter: Each February, more than a million beehives are trucked into California's almond orchards for the bloom.

zones.label: Panoche Hills
zones.text: The low Panoche Hills rise close on the west with the higher Diablo Range beyond them, and southwest of Mendota, east of the freeway, the ground sank about 28 feet from groundwater pumping.

seasons.winter: The grasslands of Panoche Valley, beyond the hills, are critical habitat, especially in winter, for golden eagles, hawks and mountain plovers.

zones.label: Firebaugh and the canals
zones.text: The aqueduct, here officially the San Luis Canal, runs through flat farmland, with the San Joaquin River and the town of Firebaugh well off to the east and the Panoche Hills to the west.

seasons.summer: Firebaugh's yearly Cantaloupe Round-Up celebrates the melon harvest, which peaks in late July.

zones.label: Los Banos and the Grasslands
zones.text: Pumping plants, power lines and canals line the west side of the valley here, while the Grasslands, a wetland of international importance on the Pacific Flyway, spread along the San Joaquin River north and east of Los Banos.

seasons.fall: Each autumn more than 20,000 cranes and 60,000 geese arrive at Merced National Wildlife Refuge to stay about six months.
seasons.spring: Wildflowers bloom in rings around the drying vernal pools of Merced National Wildlife Refuge.

zones.label: San Luis water crossroads
zones.text: The state and federal water projects meet here and share San Luis Reservoir, its dam and its forebay, while Highway 152 heads west over Pacheco Pass toward the coast.

seasons.winter: In the wet season, from about November to April, water to spare is pumped from O'Neill Forebay up into San Luis Reservoir.

zones.label: Gustine and Newman
zones.text: Two big canals run along the western edge of the valley, while farms spread east across Merced and Stanislaus counties toward the old railroad towns of Gustine and Newman and the San Joaquin River.

seasons.fall: Newman holds its yearly Fall Festival on Labor Day weekend.

zones.label: Patterson and Westley
zones.text: The Diablo Range rises close on the west, cut by Del Puerto Canyon, while Patterson, known for its distribution centers, sits east of the freeway, and on clear days Mount Diablo shows on the northwest skyline.

seasons.winter: From November through March, thick tule fog can settle over the valley floor.
seasons.summer: Downtown Patterson hosts its Apricot Fiesta on the first weekend of June.

zones.label: Tracy and the river country
zones.text: North of the I-580 junction, the freeway crosses flat San Joaquin County farmland near the edge of the Delta, between the San Joaquin River and the old railroad towns of Banta and Tracy.

seasons.fall: From autumn through spring, flocks of geese and sandhill cranes gather at the San Joaquin River refuge east of the freeway.

trivia.q: Coalinga got its name from what?
choices: A railroad stop called Coaling Station A
trivia.why: The Southern Pacific stop was called Coaling Station A, and a station sign may have squeezed it into Coalinga.

trivia.q: In Coalinga's Iron Zoo, what did Jean Dakessian Jones paint to look like animals?
trivia.why: Her Iron Zoo turned nodding oil pump jacks into animals and characters, like a zebra and a bobbing goat, to draw drivers off I-5.

trivia.q: What are the Joaquin Rocks, on the high ridge west of the freeway?
choices: A row of old oil tanks
The walls of an old fort
trivia.why: They are three pillars of rock, once called Las Tres Piedras, the Three Rocks.

trivia.q: What does Los Banos mean in Spanish?
trivia.why: The name comes from pools known as the baths of Padre Arroyo.

trivia.q: What makes San Luis Reservoir special?
choices: It is the deepest lake in the country
It is the largest offstream reservoir in the nation
It is filled with salt water
trivia.why: It is the largest offstream reservoir in the nation: most of its water is pumped in from canals instead of flowing in from a river.

trivia.q: The biggest striped bass ever caught in California came out of O'Neill Forebay in 2008. About how much did it weigh?
trivia.why: The fish, caught on August 5, 2008, was 52 and a half inches long and weighed 70.6 pounds.

trivia.q: Santa Nella's name comes from a Spanish word meaning what?
trivia.why: It is an English mangling of centinela, sentinel, from the old Rancho de Centinela.

trivia.q: The first Andersen's cafe, opened in 1924, was named in honor of what?
trivia.why: It was called Andersen's Electrical Cafe, after the couple's proudest possession, a new electric stove.

trivia.q: What poisoned the water birds at Kesterson Reservoir in the 1980s?
trivia.why: Selenium from Coast Range shale built up in farm drainage water that evaporated in the ponds.

trivia.q: In 1970, Gustine became the first place in California to have what?
trivia.why: California's first 9-1-1 system was installed in Gustine in March 1970.

trivia.q: About how many beehives are trucked into California's almond orchards each February?
trivia.why: Over a million hives, nearly half of all the hives in the country, come for the bloom.

trivia.q: Thomas Patterson laid out his town's circles and spoke-like streets after which two cities?
trivia.why: He wanted Patterson to look different from other farm towns, so he modeled it on Washington, D.C., and Paris.

trivia.q: The name Vernalis comes from a Latin word meaning what?
trivia.why: Vernalis is Latin for springlike, and a local historian said it was named for two ranchers' daughters, Verna and Alice.
